summary: K-Fire is an interactive web app that answers one question: did the fire change, or did the satellite? We unify 25+ years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (since 2000, 1 km) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m) into a single calibrated series in VIIRS S-NPP equivalents, so the sensor of origin no longer matters. Users fly from a 3D globe to a place and see a month * year burning calendar, anomalies against the historical baseline, and a Raw-Harmonized toggle that makes the artificial ~5x jump at the 2012 sensor transition disappear. Validation is published in the app: the 2012 seam shrinks from 4.95x to 1.06x, and leave-one-year-out error falls from 83% to 42%. Harmonized values are always labelled as estimates with uncertainty, and months without an active sensor are never shown as zero. The pilot covers Colombia (35 regions). It gives fire managers and scientists a trustworthy long-term baseline to judge whether a month is truly unusual.
details:
What it does
K-Fire turns two incompatible satellite records into one consistent burning-activity calendar. MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 1 km) and VIIRS (S-NPP/NOAA-20, 375 m) detect fire at very different resolutions, so raw counts jump about 5x in 2012 when VIIRS arrives, even though fire did not change. K-Fire removes that artificial step so any month from 2000 to 2026 can be compared fairly with any other.

How it works

  1. Ingest: NASA FIRMS archived detections (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m), filtered to vegetation fires with a documented confidence threshold, with persistent static heat sources removed.
  2. Count the same thing: instead of raw pixels (a sharper camera makes more pixels for the same fire), we count fire cell-days: a 1 km cell, on a given day, with at least one detection.
  3. Calibrate: a per-region, per-month “exchange rate” between sensors is learned from the 2012–2019 overlap, with shrinkage to regional or national factors where data are sparse. NOAA-20 is bridged to S-NPP the same way, and early Terra-only months are bridged to Aqua.
  4. Harmonize: one series in VIIRS S-NPP equivalents, with uncertainty bands and the source of every month stored. FRP is calibrated with a regional power-law fit.
  5. Contextualize: anomalies against a fixed 2003–2022 baseline (median, percentile, z-score classes), a composite Fire Severity Index ranking of fire clusters, ENSO and wind context, and an experimental statistical seasonal outlook clearly labelled as not an operational warning.

User experience
The app opens on a 3D globe. Users search a place or open a demo, the camera flies in, and they choose a year and month with a date picker. The calendar, map and indicators update together. A Raw/Harmonized toggle shows the 2012 seam appearing and vanishing. An AI assistant answers questions such as “Was March 2026 in Vichada unusual?” using only numbers returned by the app’s data tools, shows the filters it used, and is labelled AI-generated. Users can download a CSV and switch between English and Spanish.

Benefits and goals
We want fire managers, researchers and the public to tell real change from sensor change, and to know whether a given month is genuinely unusual. A Method tab publishes the 2012 seam test, leave-one-year-out validation, and agreement between anomaly methods. We never show burned area from hot spots, never show “no sensor” as zero, and label observed versus estimated values. Next steps are Argentina (the challenge author’s region), more countries, and spatial risk models.

Tools
Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL (globe), Apache ECharts; Python pipeline (pandas/DuckDB, scikit-learn, statsmodels) producing precomputed static JSON, so the public app does not process raw detections live; Claude via the Anthropic API for the assistant, with the API key kept server-side.
